findings.title: No verification that the authenticated user owns/belongs to the flightSchoolId or studentId supplied in the request body/query
findings.detail: Every route in this file resolves `flightSchoolId` and `studentId` directly from the client-supplied request body or query string (e.g. POST /micamp/cards L281-288, GET /micamp/cards L358-359, POST /micamp/payments L441-448, GET /micamp/payments L561-562, POST /micamp/connect L88-95, PUT /micamp/config L248, POST /micamp/disconnect L219). `requireAuth()`/`requireAdmin()` (src/server/middleware/auth.ts L153-306) only checks that a valid session exists and that its role matches an allowed list — it never binds the session's own school/tenant or student identity to the IDs used in the query. `authUser` is used only to *stamp* audit fields (`processedByUserId`, `connectedByUserId` — routes-micamp.ts L133,147,164,473,538,635,650,710,725), never as an authorization check against the resource being acted on. Any authenticated user (a student, or an admin of School A) can pass another school's `flightSchoolId` or another student's `studentId` and read/charge/tokenize/refund against it.
findings.impact: A student session can view another student's stored card metadata (GET /micamp/cards), view another student's/school's payment history (GET /micamp/payments), or — via POST /micamp/payments with useStoredCard=true — trigger a charge against another student's stored card token by supplying their studentId + flightSchoolId, since the only ownership check is 'does a card row exist matching these params' (L491-497), not 'does this card belong to the caller'. An admin session for one flight school can call requireAdmin()-gated routes (connect/disconnect/config/void/refund) against a different school's flightSchoolId with no tenant check, since requireAdmin() only checks role, not org membership. This directly violates ADR-002 (multi-tenant isolation) and is a live production issue on a billing-locked surface (real payment processor, real money).
findings.recommendation: Every route must derive the caller's own flightSchoolId (and, for student-scoped routes, verify the caller IS that studentId or an admin of that student's school) from the authenticated session — the same resolveOrgIdFromSession()/managedSchoolId pattern already used elsewhere in the codebase (referenced but never applied here) — and reject/403 when the request body's flightSchoolId/studentId doesn't match. This is a billing-locked file requiring a BILLING-APPROVED token per CLAUDE.md before modification.

findings.title: DELETE /micamp/cards/:id has no ownership check at all — any authenticated user can delete any student's stored card
findings.detail: L397-435: the route loads the card purely `where: eq(schema.studentPaymentMethods.id, cardId)` — it never checks that `card.studentId` matches the authenticated user, nor that the caller is an admin of `card.flightSchoolId`. Any authenticated user who can guess/enumerate a UUID (or gets one from another leaking endpoint) can delete any other student's stored payment method, and it also fires a live `deleteToken` call against MiCamp for that card.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant/cross-student destructive action requiring zero authorization beyond having any valid session. Could be used to grief students (delete their card right before a scheduled charge) or as a building block for further abuse.
findings.recommendation: Require `card.studentId === authUser.id` OR `authUser` is an admin/super_admin of `card.flightSchoolId` before allowing deletion.

findings.title: Void/refund transaction lookups have no flightSchoolId scoping and no idempotency guard against double-void/double-refund
findings.detail: POST /micamp/payments/:id/void (L595-660) and /refund (L662-738) load the transaction purely by `eq(schema.paymentTransactions.id, txId)` with no flightSchoolId filter tied to the admin caller's own school — any admin (of any school, since requireAdmin() doesn't check org membership per the finding above) can void or refund any transaction across the entire platform by guessing/enumerating a transaction UUID. Additionally, the refund path has no accumulation check: a transaction can be refunded multiple times as long as each individual partialAmount < transaction.amount, since status is only flipped to 'refunded' when `partialAmount >= transaction.amount` (L703) but nothing sums prior refunds against the original amount — repeated partial refunds (e.g. refund $1 nine times) could exceed the original charge with no guard, and each is a live money-movement call to MiCamp.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant unauthorized void/refund of another school's revenue. Over-refund beyond the original transaction amount is possible via repeated small partial refunds, resulting in MiCamp being asked to refund more than was ever charged (real financial loss).
findings.recommendation: Scope the transaction lookup by the admin's own flightSchoolId. Before issuing a partial refund, sum all prior completed 'refund' rows referencing this transaction's id and reject if `sum(priorRefunds) + requestedAmount > transaction.amount`.

findings.title: Void/refund calls to MiCamp are not idempotent and DB update happens after the external call with no compensation on partial failure
findings.detail: In both void (L625-652) and refund (L697-730), the sequence is: call MiCamp's live API, then update the DB. If the process crashes or the response times out between the successful MiCamp call and the DB write (or if the DB write itself fails), MiCamp has voided/refunded money but the local `paymentTransactions` row still shows `status: 'completed'` — nothing indicates the discrepancy exists, and a retry by the client would call void/refund AGAIN since the guard at L610/L679 checks the stale local status. There is no idempotency key sent to MiCamp itself (`postTransaction` in micamp.ts never includes a client-generated idempotency/reference key), so MiCamp has no way to dedupe a retried void/refund request either.
findings.impact: Double-void or double-refund on retry after a transient failure; permanent state drift between MiCamp's ledger and the local `paymentTransactions` table with no reconciliation mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the DB status update and MiCamp call in a way that tolerates partial failure — at minimum, write a 'pending' void/refund record BEFORE calling MiCamp, then finalize on success/failure, and pass an idempotency key derived from the local transaction id so a retried MiCamp call is deduped server-side.

findings.title: Bearer token cache is a single mutable instance field with no concurrency guard — concurrent requests can race on authenticate()
findings.detail: `MiCampClient.authenticate()` (L66-105) checks `this.bearerToken` / `this.tokenExpiresAt`, and on cache-miss performs an async fetch before writing the new token. Multiple concurrent calls (e.g. several simultaneous `/micamp/payments` requests for the same school, since `loadMiCampConfig` constructs a new client per-request per L59 — so this specific race is mitigated per-request, but any code path that reuses a single client instance across concurrent calls, or a future refactor that caches the MiCampClient itself, will race) will all see `bearerToken == null` simultaneously and fire N redundant authenticate calls. Not a correctness bug today because `loadMiCampConfig` creates a fresh client per request (so no shared mutable state currently), but the class itself is not safe for the caching pattern its own field names (`bearerToken`, `tokenExpiresAt`) imply, and is a latent bug if the client is ever cached/reused (a natural future optimization given the explicit `TOKEN_CACHE_MS` constant).
findings.impact: Currently benign (no shared instances), but the class's own caching design will produce redundant/racy auth calls the moment someone caches a MiCampClient across requests to reduce auth overhead — a very likely future change given the code already computed a 55-minute cache window that is never actually exploited across requests.
findings.recommendation: Either remove the misleading token-cache fields until an actual shared-instance pattern is introduced, or if adding one, guard `authenticate()` with an in-flight promise so concurrent callers await the same authentication request.

findings.title: Processing fee and dollar-amount conversion uses floating point arithmetic, risking off-by-a-cent charges
findings.detail: L476-481: `processingFee = Math.round(amount * (feePercent / 100))` is fine (rounds to integer cents), but `amountDollars = totalCharged / 100` performs floating-point division that can produce values like `19.990000000000002` for `totalCharged = 1999`. This value is sent directly to MiCamp as `Amount` (micamp.ts `Sale`/`Refund`/`saleWithToken` request bodies) without any `.toFixed(2)` normalization — relying on JSON.stringify + the downstream JSON parser/gateway to coerce it correctly. Similarly `refundAmountDollars = refundAmountCents / 100` at L695 has the same issue.
findings.impact: Most cent values convert cleanly, but certain amounts are documented IEEE-754 cases that don't round-trip cleanly through `/100`, risking a malformed amount being sent to a live payment gateway (either rejected, or charged as a slightly different amount than displayed to the user/recorded in totalCharged).
findings.recommendation: Normalize dollar amounts sent to MiCamp with `Number((cents / 100).toFixed(2))` (or format as a fixed 2-decimal string if the API accepts one) before sending, both in routes-micamp.ts and centrally inside micamp.ts's sale/refund/saleWithToken methods so every caller gets the guard.

findings.title: Card expiration year parsing assumes 2-digit YY always maps to 20YY with no century rollover guard, and malformed input silently produces NaN stored to the DB
findings.detail: L318-321: `expirationDate` is taken from the client with zero format validation (no regex check that it's MM/YY or MMYY before use). `expClean.slice(0,2)` / `expClean.slice(2)` are parsed via `Number.parseInt` with no bounds checking — if `expirationDate` is malformed (e.g. wrong length, non-numeric, single digit), `expMonth`/`expYear` become `NaN` and are inserted directly into `studentPaymentMethods.expMonth`/`expYear` (both `integer().notNull()` per schema — a NaN insert will either throw a generic DB error surfaced as a 502 to the user, masking the real validation problem, or in JS/pg driver serialization NaN may coerce unpredictably). There's also no check that `expMonth` is 1-12 or that the card isn't already expired.
findings.impact: Malformed or already-expired card data can be tokenized and stored; errors surface as opaque 502s from the DB layer rather than a clear 400 validation error, making debugging harder and allowing garbage data into a billing-critical table.
findings.recommendation: Validate `expirationDate` matches `/^\d{2}\/?\d{2}$/`, that month is 1-12, and that the resulting expiration date is not in the past, before calling MiCamp or inserting into the DB. Return 400 on failure.

findings.title: Duplicate stored-card insert bypasses the DB unique constraint's intended replace semantics — old token is never revoked
findings.detail: `studentPaymentMethods` has a unique index on `(studentId, flightSchoolId, processor)` (schema/index.ts L7017-7019), meaning a student can only have one micamp card row. But POST /micamp/cards (L323-337) does a plain `.insert(...)` with no `onConflictDoUpdate` — if a student adds a second card, this insert will throw a unique-constraint violation from Postgres, which is caught generically at L349-353 and surfaced as an opaque 502 'Payment tokenization error' rather than a clear 'you already have a card on file, delete it first' message. Worse, if a caller relies on 'insert new card = replace old', the old MiCamp token is silently orphaned (never deleted via `deleteToken`), leaking a live tokenized card at the processor that the local system has lost track of.
findings.impact: Confusing 502 error on legitimate card-replacement attempts; orphaned card tokens left live at MiCamp with no local record to ever clean them up (delete-token happens only through the explicit DELETE /micamp/cards/:id route, which requires knowing the local row id).
findings.recommendation: Use `onConflictDoUpdate` on `(studentId, flightSchoolId, processor)` in the cards insert, and inside that transaction call `deleteToken()` on the previous token to avoid orphaning it at MiCamp — mirroring the pattern already used in `/micamp/connect` (L152-171).

findings.title: Invoice number defaults to `pay-${Date.now()}` with no uniqueness guarantee under concurrent requests
findings.detail: L484: when `invoiceId` is not supplied, `InvoiceNumber` falls back to `pay-${Date.now()}` (millisecond resolution). Two concurrent payment requests for the same student within the same millisecond (plausible under retry/double-click without a debounce) would generate the same InvoiceNumber sent to MiCamp, and there is no client-side idempotency key preventing the underlying `/micamp/payments` POST from being processed twice on a network-retry (e.g. a client timeout that retries the same POST) — nothing in `postTransaction` submits a de-dup token, so a retried request is a brand-new charge.
findings.impact: Duplicate charge risk on client retry (e.g. double-tap 'Pay Now', or a fetch timeout retry) with no server-side idempotency protection.
findings.recommendation: Require the client to generate and pass an idempotency key (UUID) for POST /micamp/payments, and check for an existing paymentTransactions row with the same key before calling MiCamp again; replace `Date.now()`-based invoice numbers with a UUID or DB-sequence-derived value.

findings.title: GET /micamp/admin/schools does an in-memory N-table join instead of a SQL join, and returns processing fee percent + merchant key for every school with no pagination
findings.detail: L771-811: fetches ALL flight schools and ALL micamp configs as two separate full-table scans, then joins them in application memory via a Map. As the number of flight schools grows this becomes an unbounded, unpaginated payload with two full-table reads per request (super-admin only, so lower severity, but still a scalability smell in a route intended to list every tenant on the platform).
findings.impact: Linear growth in response size and latency as schools onboard; no pagination means the endpoint will eventually become slow or hit response-size limits.
findings.recommendation: Do a single SQL LEFT JOIN between flightSchools and paymentProcessorConfigs filtered to processor='micamp', and add pagination/limit params once school count grows past a reasonable threshold (e.g. 200).

findings.title: postTransaction's declined-response parsing assumes JSON body always parses cleanly and always has the expected shape
findings.detail: L282: `const data = await response.json();` has no try/catch of its own separate from the outer try/catch — if MiCamp ever returns a non-JSON body (HTML error page, empty body, gateway timeout page from a proxy in front of MiCamp) on a 5xx, `response.json()` throws a JSON parse error, which IS caught by the outer catch (L296-300) and re-thrown as a generic `[MiCamp] Transaction error: SyntaxError: Unexpected token...` — functionally survives, but the resulting error message is unhelpful for on-call debugging of a real payment failure, and it's indistinguishable from a genuine card decline in the caller's generic 502 handler in routes-micamp.ts.
findings.impact: Poor observability into payment-gateway outages vs actual declines; on-call must read a cryptic JSON parse error to infer 'MiCamp itself was down' rather than getting a clear signal.
findings.recommendation: Check `response.ok` before attempting to parse JSON for the success path, and wrap the `response.json()` call to produce a distinct error class/message (e.g. 'MiCamp gateway returned non-JSON response, status {status}') so downstream monitoring/alerting can distinguish gateway outages from declines.

findings.title: migration-manifest.ts is stale and silently desyncs from the journal on every migration-only commit — feeds a Sentry health check that will false-fire
findings.detail: src/generated/migration-manifest.ts is a committed, hand-frozen snapshot (MIGRATION_COUNT = 416, LATEST_MIGRATION = '0424_rate_null_subject_uniqueness') generated by scripts/generate-migration-manifest.js. That script is wired ONLY to `prebuild` (package.json:11), which runs during `npm run build`, not during migration-only commits or via any pre-push/CI gate. The journal (drizzle/meta/_journal.json) currently has 418 entries with the true latest tag `0426_register_atp_frc_analytics_v2_flags` — the manifest is stale by 2 entries and 2 tags behind right now. src/lib/db-health.ts:21 does an exact-equality check `appliedCount !== MIGRATION_COUNT` and fires `Sentry.captureMessage(..., 'error')` on any mismatch. Nothing forces the manifest to be regenerated+committed alongside a migration PR, so it drifts on essentially every migration-adding PR that doesn't happen to run a full `npm run build` before commit. The 'expected' count is also environment-dependent in a way a single hardcoded constant can never represent: several journal tags are stub/orphan entries (0036__pre_push_check, 0050__pre_push_check, 0057__pre_push_check, 0067__pre_push_check) whose SQL files may or may not exist per environment (db-migrate.ts skips tracking them if the file is missing).
findings.impact: Either Sentry fires a false 'error' on every deploy purely because the manifest wasn't rebuilt after the last migration PR (alert fatigue, real signal ignored), or the frozen count coincidentally matches a broken DB state and a genuine missing-migration incident goes unreported. Either way the check defeats its stated purpose of ops visibility into migration drift.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) stop comparing to a static frozen number — compute expected count directly from drizzle/meta/_journal.json at runtime, or (2) add a CI/pre-push step that regenerates the manifest and fails if `git diff --exit-code src/generated/migration-manifest.ts` is non-clean, matching the existing schema-drift/orphan-migration/orphan-snapshot pattern already in .husky/pre-push. No such check currently exists for this file.

findings.title: Journal idx numbers do not match their SQL filename's numeric prefix for two entries (0089/0091 swapped) — no guard rail catches this class of drift
findings.detail: In drizzle/meta/_journal.json, journal idx 89 maps to tag `0091_add_workflow_canvas_fields` and idx 91 maps to tag `0089_add_stage_check_tables` — the idx field and the filename's own numeric prefix disagree for these two entries. This is the same class of ordering corruption that produced multiple emergency repair blocks in scripts/db-migrate.ts (e.g. the 0075/0174, 0079/0080, 0132/0133 timestamp-skip blocks address symptoms of out-of-order/mismatched journal entries). The pre-push hook has orphan-file, orphan-snapshot, and cross-branch index-conflict checks, but nothing validates a journal entry's idx matches its own tag's numeric filename prefix.
findings.impact: drizzle-orm applies migrations in journal-array order (not filename-prefix order), gated on `when` timestamp vs the tracking table's max created_at. A human skimming drizzle/*.sql filenames to reason about apply order will draw the wrong conclusion for this pair. Low blast radius today (both entries are already tracked/applied everywhere per the repair-probe history), but a landmine for the next person diagnosing an out-of-order migration bug.
findings.recommendation: Add a cheap static check (alongside the existing `drizzle-kit check` step) asserting `entry.idx === parseInt(entry.tag.split('_')[0], 10)` for every journal entry. Fix these two entries if renumbering is judged safe, or document the known exception if renumbering churn isn't worth it (both are fully applied everywhere already).

findings.title: scripts/db-migrate.ts has grown to ~2,400 lines of hand-written, per-migration repair special-cases — high-risk single point of maintenance
findings.detail: The file contains dozens of hardcoded, narrative-commented repair blocks (one per historically-broken migration: 0021, 0035/0039, 0061, 0064/0083, 0069, 0075/0174, 0076/0077, 0078/0082, 0079/0080, 0099/0100, 0104, 0116/0117/0123/0126, 0132/0133/0141, 0159, 0173, 0175, 0221/0223/0227, 0294, 0296, 0314, 0315/0316, 0341/0342, plus generic table/column/constraint probe arrays) — each embedding full CREATE TABLE / ALTER TABLE DDL duplicated from the original migration files. Understandable as an incremental response to real production incidents (each block cites a specific postmortem/symptom), but every new probe increases the risk that a future schema change to one of these tables silently diverges from its embedded repair-DDL twin.
findings.impact: Not an active bug today — every probe correctly gates on existence before running idempotent DDL. Forward-looking risk: no automated signal ties a real migration edit to its duplicate repair-DDL snippet, and the ever-growing probe list adds information_schema/pg_catalog query overhead to every migration run, even on fully healthy databases where no probe ever fires.
findings.recommendation: Not urgent. Consider extracting probe arrays into one declarative config consumed by a generic runner (already mostly true for array-based probes), and short-circuit all probes once `areAllMigrationsTracked()` returns true, since a fully-tracked DB cannot need any repair by definition — this removes the per-run query overhead on well-behaved environments.

findings.title: Reconciliation confirm always reports 'matched' even when the update touched zero rows
findings.detail: matchInvoiceToExisting (line ~1845-1871) and matchPaymentToExisting (line ~1873-1898) run `db.update(...).where(...)` with no `.returning()` and no row-count check, then do `return updated !== null;`. Drizzle's neon-serverless update() always resolves to a query result object, never `null` — so this check is always true regardless of whether the WHERE clause (matchId + flightSchoolId + isNull(stripeInvoiceId)) actually matched a row. If the admin's decision.matchId is stale, wrong, or the target invoice/payment already has a Stripe id attached (so the `isNull(...)` guard excludes it), the update silently no-ops but the caller (confirmStudentStripeReconciliation, routes-stripe.ts POST /stripe/customers/:studentId/reconciliation/confirm) still reports status 'matched' and increments result.matched.
findings.impact: Admin performing manual reconciliation is told a Stripe invoice/payment was linked to a local record when it was not. The record stays unmatched (no stripeInvoiceId/stripePaymentIntentId), so it resurfaces as brand_new/suggested_match in the next preview, or worse, the admin believes reconciliation is complete while the local ledger and Stripe stay out of sync — a silent accounting drift in a billing-adjacent feature.
findings.recommendation: Check actual affected row count: add `.returning({ id: ... })` and check the returned array length, or inspect the result's rowCount/count property for the exact driver in use, instead of `!== null`.

findings.title: Webhook idempotency-insert fallback path is a non-atomic check-then-insert race
findings.detail: insertStripeWebhookReceipt() (lines 170-207) branches on `typeof insertBuilder.onConflictDoNothing === 'function'`. The real production driver (NeonDatabase from drizzle-orm/neon-serverless, confirmed via src/lib/db.ts) always exposes onConflictDoNothing, so the atomic upsert-guard path is always taken in production. The fallback branch (find-then-insert, no transaction, no reliance on the unique constraint) only executes against a test/mock db lacking that method, and is a genuine TOCTOU race if two webhook redeliveries land concurrently against that mock.
findings.impact: No production impact — the fallback is unreachable there. Only matters if a future refactor swaps the db client to something lacking onConflictDoNothing, or the mock is reused as a stand-in for a real environment.
findings.recommendation: Delete the dead fallback branch (fail loudly if onConflictDoNothing is missing) or add a comment stating explicitly it is test-only and unsafe for concurrent production use, since the unique index stripe_webhook_events_owner_provider_event_uniq is what actually guarantees idempotency in production.

findings.title: customer.updated webhook can silently overwrite a student's email with an unverified value from Stripe, with no audit trail
findings.detail: handleCustomerUpdated (lines 1291-1320) mirrors any non-empty Stripe customer.email onto the matched ATOS user.email whenever it differs (case-insensitively) from the current value, with no validation, no confirmation step, and no audit log entry — every other webhook handler in this file writes to auditLogs; this one does not.
findings.impact: Any actor who can edit the Stripe customer object on the school's Connect account (school-side Stripe dashboard user, or a compromised/misconfigured integration) can silently change a student's login/notification email in ATOS with zero audit trail. Given PDD-006's stated concern that Stripe-side data is less trustworthy than ATOS-owned data, this is an unreviewed one-way trust boundary from Stripe into an auth-adjacent column.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, write an auditLogs row (matching the pattern used by every other handler in this file) recording old/new email and the triggering event id. Consider whether email should be mirrored unattended at all given it's auth-relevant, or gate it behind an admin review queue.

findings.title: handleDisputeCreated contains dead code (always-null piPaymentMethod branch) and an unnecessary dynamic import of an already-imported module
findings.detail: Lines 908-942: piPaymentMethod is computed via a ternary that is provably always null (`typeof dispute.payment_intent === 'object' && dispute.payment_intent ? null : null`), then immediately voided with `void piPaymentMethod` to suppress the unused-var lint. The actual PM-blocking logic instead re-fetches the charge via a dynamic `import('@/lib/stripe')` even though stripeClient is already imported at module scope.
findings.impact: No functional bug — the real block logic works via the charge lookup — but the dead ternary and duplicate/dynamic import are a maintenance trap; a future editor could assume piPaymentMethod does something.
findings.recommendation: Delete piPaymentMethod and the void line entirely; replace the dynamic `await import('@/lib/stripe')` with the module-level stripeClient import.

findings.title: Duplicate Stripe customer-search implementations between routes-stripe.ts and school-stripe-service.ts
findings.detail: findCandidateCustomers() in routes-stripe.ts (lines 244-324) and findCustomerCandidates() in school-stripe-service.ts (lines 449-508) implement nearly identical customer.list/customer.search + Promise.allSettled + de-dupe logic independently, but only the routes-stripe.ts version includes confidence scoring, phone matching, and failOnSearchError behavior.
findings.impact: Two near-duplicate implementations of Stripe customer search increase the chance the two drift (e.g., a future name-search injection fix or Stripe API param change applied to one and not the other) — directly inside the PDD-006-protected duplicate-detection surface.
findings.recommendation: Consolidate on the more complete routes-stripe.ts implementation, or remove the unused SchoolStripeService.findCustomerCandidates method if nothing calls it.

result.notes: Enumerated every file in the owned slice: routes-stripe.ts (2411 lines), stripe-webhook/route.ts (1391 lines), school-stripe-service.ts (2637 lines), stripe-client-factory.ts, stripe-circuit-breaker.ts, stripe-encryption.ts, stripe-integration-recovery.ts, stripe-integration-status.ts, stripe-errors.ts, retrieve-customer-with-fallback.ts, stripe-mapping-sweep-cron/route.ts, and both /pay client pages + their payment-client.tsx components. The small utility files (encryption, circuit breaker, client factory, integration status/recovery, errors) are clean — correct AES-256-GCM implementation, proper cache TTL/invalidation, sound Connect-mode gating. PDD-006's admin-gating (requireAdmin on /stripe/customers/sync, force-create reason enum, audit trail via auditStripeSync) is correctly implemented and enforced at every mutation path traced, including sweep and link-direct. The tenant-isolation pattern (ensureStudentFlightSchoolAccess, assertCustomerBoundary against school Connect account) is consistently applied across all customer-mapping routes. No SQL injection, no missing auth, no cross-tenant leak found in this slice. The /pay/* client components call routes outside this slice's ownership (/api/server/pay/*) so were reviewed only for in-slice concerns (none found — they correctly use the `focus` event, not `visibilitychange`, per the project's banned-pattern rule).

findings.title: Row-Level Security tenant isolation is fully deployed at the DB but never activated by application code
findings.detail: Migration 0144 enables RLS with tenant_isolation/tenant_insert policies on ~80 tenant-scoped tables, gated on current_setting('app.flight_school_id') via get_current_flight_school_id(). The only application code that ever calls set_config('app.flight_school_id', ...) is setTenantContext() in src/lib/db-tenant-context.ts — and a repo-wide grep shows setTenantContext/clearTenantContext have zero callers anywhere in src/. Every real query therefore executes with app.flight_school_id unset (NULL). Cross-checked routes-stripe.ts: tenant scoping there is done entirely via explicit flightSchoolId !== callerOrgId checks in application code, not RLS.
findings.impact: The migration comment and function docstrings assert RLS is 'the mechanism that prevents cross-org data leakage,' but it is not wired up. Any application-code bug that omits a WHERE flight_school_id = ... filter has no DB-level backstop. This is exactly the class of incident ADR-002 exists to prevent, and the safety net is currently a no-op.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) wire setTenantContext/clearTenantContext into the actual request path (Hono middleware, per-request, before any query) and verify the connection pooling model actually preserves session-local GUCs per logical request (see next finding), or (2) if RLS is intentionally not used and app-layer WHERE clauses are the real control, remove/document the RLS migration and dead functions so nobody trusts a phantom backstop.

findings.title: Even if activated, setTenantContext's session GUC cannot be safely used with the shared connection Pool
findings.detail: db (src/lib/db.ts:59) is a lazy Drizzle client over a shared @neondatabase/serverless Pool (max 8 connections). setTenantContext calls db.execute(sql`SELECT set_config(..., true)`) — set_config with is_local=true is transaction-scoped and reverts on whichever physical connection serviced that call. Drizzle's pooled db.execute checks out an arbitrary connection per call; there's no pool.connect() + pinned client per logical request/transaction here. Even if setTenantContext were called, the next query for the same 'session' could land on a different pooled connection with no tenant context set, or inherit stale context left by a prior request that was never cleared.
findings.impact: RLS-via-session-GUC as currently structured is fundamentally unsafe under connection pooling: it can silently apply the wrong tenant's context to a query, or none at all. This is a correctness bug waiting to be exploited the moment someone 'fixes' the dead-code issue above by calling setTenantContext from middleware without also re-architecting connection handling.
findings.recommendation: If RLS is to be the real enforcement mechanism, tenant context must be set on a per-transaction basis using a pinned client (pool.connect() -> set_config -> run all tenant queries on that client -> release), or set at the start of every db.transaction() callback, never on the ambient pooled db. Otherwise keep RLS as documentation-only and rely solely on the application-level flightSchoolId checks that are actually doing the work today.

findings.title: check:tenant-guard CI gate is defined but never invoked by pre-push or CI workflows
findings.detail: scripts/check-tenant-write-guard.ts implements two real regression gates (derive-from-URL org guard, hardcoded PII roster) and is registered as npm run check:tenant-guard (package.json:42). Grepping .husky/pre-push and .github/workflows/*.yml for check:tenant-guard / check-tenant-write-guard returns no matches — the gate is not called from the pre-push hook or from any CI workflow.
findings.impact: The exact class of regression this script exists to catch (hardcoded roster, derive-from-URL missing org guard — both explicitly cited in the script's own header comment as prior incidents) can be reintroduced and merged without this check ever running.
findings.recommendation: Add npm run check:tenant-guard to .husky/pre-push (alongside the existing migration-journal check) and/or a CI workflow step, so it actually blocks the regressions it was built to catch.

findings.title: Soft-delete read filter helpers exist and are tested but have zero production callers
findings.detail: notDeleted()/liveAnd() (src/server/db/soft-delete.ts) are the designated shared filter for excluding soft-deleted (deleted_at IS NOT NULL) rows, per the file's own doc comment: 'the internal Hono routes and the repository layer do not [filter], so once soft-delete is rolled out, those reads would leak archived rows back into the UI.' A repo-wide grep for notDeleted( / liveAnd( outside the test file and definition file returns zero results.
findings.impact: 12 tables carry a deleted_at column (per drizzle/*.sql), implying soft-delete is at least partially rolled out at the schema level, but the documented required read-filter is not applied anywhere in application code. Archived/soft-deleted rows can surface in live queries and the UI.
findings.recommendation: Audit every table with a deleted_at column, confirm whether soft-delete is actually relied upon, and wire notDeleted/liveAnd into the corresponding repository read paths. If soft-delete isn't live yet, update the doc comment so it doesn't read as an already-broken guarantee.

findings.title: idempotency_keys table has no tenant scoping — global key namespace across all flight schools
findings.detail: The idempotency_keys table (drizzle/0142) has PK key varchar(255) with no flight_school_id/tenant column, and withIdempotency() (src/lib/idempotency.ts:9) looks up/stores purely by the caller-supplied key string with no tenant qualifier. If any caller derives the idempotency key from client-controllable or non-globally-unique input, one flight school's request could collide with another's key and receive a cached response containing a different tenant's data.
findings.impact: Cross-tenant response leakage if two different flight schools' requests ever produce the same idempotency key. Currently zero callers found for withIdempotency( outside its own definition, so not yet exploitable, but it is landmine dead code waiting for the first caller.
findings.recommendation: Add a flight_school_id column to idempotency_keys, include it in the lookup/insert WHERE and uniqueness constraint, and require callers to pass the tenant id explicitly. Compare to accounting_provider_idempotency_keys (drizzle/0346) which correctly scopes by owner_type, owner_id, provider, ... — follow that pattern.

findings.title: withIdempotency has a check-then-act race: concurrent duplicate requests both execute the handler
findings.detail: withIdempotency (src/lib/idempotency.ts:9-42) does a plain SELECT for an existing key, and if absent, runs handler() then INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING. Between the SELECT and the INSERT there is no lock/transaction — two concurrent requests with the same idempotency key will both see 'no existing row', both execute handler(), and race on the INSERT: the loser's real result is silently discarded and it returns cached: false with its own executed-but-orphaned result, not the winner's actual persisted response.
findings.impact: If used for a non-idempotent operation (payment capture, record creation) under concurrent retry — exactly the scenario idempotency keys exist to guard against — the handler can run twice, defeating the utility's purpose. No production callers found currently, so impact is latent.
findings.recommendation: Use an atomic INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING * up front to claim the key before running the handler, or wrap check+insert in a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / advisory lock on the key, so only one concurrent caller executes the handler.

findings.title: Startup schema-drift probe applies ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN outside the migration/journal system
findings.detail: runSchemaDriftProbe() (src/lib/db-startup-probe.ts:114) runs at server startup, diffs live information_schema.columns against the Drizzle schema, and executes ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS directly against production — including dynamically creating enum types (ensureEnumType) — completely outside drizzle/*.sql + _journal.json. Runs on a separate, unpooled new Pool({ connectionString: url }) with no retry/circuit-breaker wrapping, on every cold start until it succeeds once per instance.
findings.impact: This directly contradicts PDD-008 ('missing journal entries caused production 500s') by providing a second, silent, non-journaled path for schema changes to land in production. A column added this way exists in the DB but has no corresponding migration file/journal entry, so the migration-count health check would not catch drift. Schema state can also differ across environments depending on which one runs the probe first.
findings.recommendation: Flag to the team rather than change unilaterally (Destructive Action Guard). At minimum this should alert loudly (not just console.log) whenever it actually applies a column change in production; ideally convert the safety-net into a CI drift check that fails the build, with the real fix always going through a proper Drizzle migration + journal entry.

findings.title: db-health.ts migration-count check silently swallows errors and Sentry-init failures in production
findings.detail: assertMigrationsUpToDate() (src/lib/db-health.ts:13) catches all errors in production and only logs to console + best-effort Sentry, itself wrapped in a swallowed try/catch (lines 25-29 and 34-38). If the query fails in production (drizzle schema missing, permission denied, connectivity issue), this returns silently with no distinction from 'check ran and passed'.
findings.impact: Low — health-check nicety, not a data-integrity path. But the double-swallow makes it possible for a check meant to give 'ops visibility' to fail completely invisibly if Sentry also throws at the same time the DB query fails.
findings.recommendation: Distinguish 'check ran and passed', 'check ran and found mismatch', and 'check could not run' in the log line/metric so silent failure-to-check doesn't look identical to a clean pass.

findings.title: syncPaymentToQuickBooks discards existing invoiceUrl, destroying prior data on every payment sync
findings.detail: In `syncPaymentToQuickBooks` (src/lib/quickbooks-sync.ts:409-413), after building `updatedMeta` from the existing parsed metadata, the code calls `buildQBUrl(null, updatedMeta)` instead of `buildQBUrl(invoice.invoiceUrl, updatedMeta)`. `buildQBUrl` (lines 77-83) preserves any pre-existing non-QB URL (e.g. a Stripe hosted invoice link) by prefixing it before the `qb:` metadata suffix, but only when the caller passes the existing URL. Passing `null` always collapses `invoiceUrl` down to just the bare `qb:{...}` JSON blob, silently wiping out whatever was stored before every time a payment is synced.
findings.impact: Any Stripe-hosted-invoice link or other data previously appended to `invoiceUrl` is permanently lost the first time a payment syncs to QuickBooks for that invoice. Downstream UI/consumers reading `invoiceUrl` for a Stripe link will silently break after payment sync.
findings.recommendation: Change line 412 to `buildQBUrl(invoice.invoiceUrl, updatedMeta)` so the existing URL prefix is preserved. Add a unit test that seeds `invoice.invoiceUrl` with both a plain URL and prior `qb:` metadata, syncs a payment, and asserts the original prefix survives.

findings.title: findCustomerByName uses non-functional escaping for QBO query strings — malformed queries for names containing apostrophes
findings.detail: `findCustomerByName` (src/lib/quickbooks.ts:343-348) escapes single quotes with `name.replace(/'/g, "\\'")` (backslash-escape) before embedding into a QBO SQL-like query string: `SELECT * FROM Customer WHERE DisplayName = '${escaped}'`. QuickBooks Online's query language does not support backslash-escaping of quotes — it follows standard SQL convention where a literal single quote is escaped by doubling it (`''`). A sibling QBO integration in the same codebase, `src/server/assistant/tools/native/qbo.ts` (line 140-141, `escapeQboString`), correctly doubles the quote and is verified by a test asserting `DisplayName = 'O''Hare'`.
findings.impact: Any flight school whose name contains an apostrophe (e.g. "O'Brien Aviation") will send a malformed query to the QBO API, throwing a query-parse error and breaking `findOrCreateQBCustomer` → invoice sync fails for that school.
findings.recommendation: Replace `name.replace(/'/g, "\\'")` with `name.replace(/'/g, "''")`, or extract a shared `escapeQboString` helper reused by both `src/lib/quickbooks.ts` and `src/server/assistant/tools/native/qbo.ts`. Add a unit test mirroring the existing `qbo.test.ts` apostrophe case.

findings.title: qb_entity_map has no DB-level unique constraint despite comments claiming one; insert() has a check-then-act race
findings.detail: `src/lib/schema/quickbooks.ts` line 91 comments the `atosEntityIdx` as "Critical: composite unique enforces one mapping per ATOS entity per school", but it is defined via `index(...)` (lines 92-96), not `.unique()` — Drizzle's `index()` builder produces a plain non-unique btree index. There is no DB constraint preventing two rows with the same `(flightSchoolId, atosEntityId, atosEntityType)`. `qbEntityMapRepo.insert()` (src/repositories/quickbooks/qbEntityMapRepo.ts:126-165) does a `SELECT` (`findLegacy`) to check for an existing row and only inserts if none is found — a check-then-act race with no transaction/advisory lock.
findings.impact: Two concurrent sync attempts for the same ATOS entity (e.g. a webhook-triggered CDC sync racing a manual admin sync) can both pass the `findLegacy` check before either inserts, producing duplicate `qb_entity_map` rows for the same entity. Downstream lookups use `.limit(1)` with no ordering, so which mapping 'wins' is nondeterministic — potential double-posting to QuickBooks or SyncToken confusion (stale-token write failures, per the file's own doc comment on line 69).
findings.recommendation: Add a real unique index (Drizzle `uniqueIndex`) on `(flight_school_id, atos_entity_id, atos_entity_type)` and use `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`/`DO UPDATE` in `insert()` instead of check-then-insert, mirroring the idempotent pattern already used correctly in `qbWebhookEventRepo.insertIfNew`.

findings.title: syncInvoiceToQuickBooks / syncPaymentToQuickBooks call qbConnectionRepo.findActive() as a gate but then use a disconnected legacy user-scoped token store
findings.detail: `syncInvoiceToQuickBooks` (src/lib/quickbooks-sync.ts:205) and `syncPaymentToQuickBooks` (line 351) both call `await qbConnectionRepo.findActive(invoice.flightSchoolId)` — which throws `QBNotConnectedError` if the school has no active row in the newer, school-scoped `qb_connections` table — but never use the returned connection object. Both functions then call `QuickBooksClient.create(qbUserId)` (src/lib/quickbooks.ts:153), which reads tokens from the entirely separate, legacy, per-*user* `userIntegrations` table. The `findActive()` call functions only as a gate while the actual API calls run against a different, disconnected credential store scoped by user rather than by school.
findings.impact: A school could pass the `findActive` gate (active `qb_connections` row) yet have no `userIntegrations` row for the given `qbUserId`, causing `QuickBooksClient.create` to throw a confusing 'No QuickBooks integration found for user' error that masks the real cause. The two-token-store split (confirmed by `LEGACY_QB_REPLACEMENT` messaging and `ENABLE_LEGACY_USER_SCOPED_QB_SYNC` flag in routes-quickbooks.ts) is a known-in-progress migration, but `quickbooks-sync.ts` layers the new gate on top of the old token flow without reconciling them.
findings.recommendation: Either (a) make these functions actually consume the `QbConnection` row returned by `findActive()` to build the QB client, fully migrating off `userIntegrations`, or (b) if superseded by `qbInvoiceSyncService`/`qbPaymentSyncService` (referenced in routes-quickbooks.ts as the new path), delete the unused `findActive()` call and clearly mark `quickbooks-sync.ts` as legacy-only.

findings.title: Process-local in-memory state (customerCache, recentErrors, lastSyncTime) is unsafe on serverless/multi-instance deployment
findings.detail: `customerCache` (line 88), `lastSyncTime` (line 92), and `recentErrors` (lines 93-98) are module-level variables holding process-local state, used by `findOrCreateQBCustomer`, `syncInvoiceToQuickBooks`, `syncPaymentToQuickBooks`, and surfaced via `getSyncStatus()` (used by `/quickbooks/sync/status`).
findings.impact: On Vercel/serverless, each invocation may run in a different or freshly cold-started context, so `customerCache` provides no reliable cross-request benefit and can serve a stale QB customer ID after a customer merge/dedup in QBO. `lastSyncTime`/`recentErrors` reported by the sync dashboard are inconsistent per-instance and lose all history on cold start — exactly what the newer `qb_sync_log` table with its `/quickbooks/diagnostics` endpoint was built to replace.
findings.recommendation: If `quickbooks-sync.ts` remains active, replace `customerCache` with a persisted lookup (e.g. `qb_entity_map` keyed by `atosEntityType='customer'`) and replace `recentErrors`/`lastSyncTime` with a query against `qb_sync_log`.

findings.title: Legacy QuickBooks OAuth flow is gated by a single global env var with no per-tenant scoping, and defaults enabled in test env
findings.detail: `legacyUserScopedQuickBooksEnabled()` (src/server/routes/routes-quickbooks.ts:117-123) gates the entire legacy OAuth/callback/sync/disconnect flow behind one process-wide `ENABLE_LEGACY_USER_SCOPED_QB_SYNC` env var for all schools and users simultaneously; there is no per-school migration flag, and the flag defaults true in `NODE_ENV === 'test'`.
findings.impact: Low likelihood but non-trivial blast radius: an accidental flip of this single flag in production re-opens `/quickbooks/auth-url`, `/quickbooks/callback`, `/quickbooks/sync/*` for all tenants at once, potentially creating `userIntegrations` rows that diverge from the intended `qb_connections`/`accounting_provider_connections` system of record, and re-exposes the invoiceUrl-discard and query-escaping bugs above.
findings.recommendation: Once the migration off the legacy path is confirmed complete, remove the legacy routes/flag entirely rather than leaving a global kill-switch that can silently reactivate a superseded subsystem.

findings.title: Schema comment documents a 4-part encrypted-token format that neither decrypt() implementation in this slice matches
findings.detail: `src/lib/schema/quickbooks.ts:40` documents the `qb_connections` encrypted token format as `${iv}:${tag}:${data}:${version}` (4 parts including a version segment). Both `decrypt()` implementations in this slice (`src/lib/quickbooks.ts:46-55` and `src/server/routes/routes-quickbooks.ts:78-87`) destructure only 3 parts with no version field, and their paired `encrypt()` functions only ever produce 3-part strings.
findings.impact: Low direct impact since the 3-part functions are internally self-consistent, but the stale 4-part comment on the `qb_connections` table (written to by out-of-slice token-service code, not these two files) could mislead a future developer implementing key-rotation/version-aware decryption, or mask that the two parallel QB token stores use different encryption code paths that happen to currently produce the same 3-part shape.
findings.recommendation: Verify against the out-of-slice `qbTokenService.ts` whether a 4-part format is actually produced there; if not, fix the comment in `src/lib/schema/quickbooks.ts` to match reality.

findings.title: Owned-path scan target src/app/api/quickbooks-callback does not exist in the repository
findings.detail: The scan mandate lists `src/app/api/quickbooks-callback` as an owned path, but no such directory exists. The actual QB OAuth callback lives at `src/app/api/integrations/qbo/callback/route.ts` (part of the newer `accounting_provider_connections`-based integration, outside this slice's literal file list), and the frontend callback landing page is `src/components/features/mvp-v2/pages/quickbooks-callback.tsx`. The legacy callback logic lives inline in `src/server/routes/routes-quickbooks.ts` (`POST /quickbooks/callback`, already reviewed).
findings.impact: Not a code defect — flagging so the scan orchestrator can correct the slice's owned-path list; nothing was left unscanned because nothing exists at the listed path.
findings.recommendation: Update the scan configuration to point at `src/app/api/integrations/qbo/callback/route.ts` and `src/components/features/mvp-v2/pages/quickbooks-callback.tsx` if they should be covered by this or another slice.

findings.title: /delete-user has no tenant scoping — any flight-school admin can delete any user account platform-wide
findings.detail: POST /delete-user (routes-auth.ts:879-939) is guarded only by requireAdmin() (role check: admin OR super_admin). Unlike the sibling endpoint /update-user-metadata (line 1046, which explicitly calls resolveSameOrgAuthUser to confirm the target belongs to the caller's school before writing), /delete-user resolves the target purely from the caller-supplied email or userId and calls auth.api.removeUser({ body: { userId: resolvedUserId } }) with zero org/tenant check. A regular flight-school 'admin' (not super_admin) can supply any other school's user email, or even another school's admin, and delete that account.
findings.impact: A single compromised or malicious flight-school admin account can delete arbitrary users across every tenant on the platform, including other schools' admins. This is a cross-tenant destructive action with no audit gate beyond the requireAdmin() role check, directly contradicting PDD-005's multi-tenant isolation intent and the pattern this file itself establishes elsewhere (resolveSameOrgAuthUser).
findings.recommendation: Call resolveSameOrgAuthUser(c, authUser, resolvedUserId) before invoking auth.api.removeUser, mirroring /update-user-metadata, and return 403 when it returns null. Reserve cross-tenant deletes for requireSuperAdmin().

findings.title: emergency-password-reset does not revoke existing sessions or force a password change
findings.detail: POST /emergency-password-reset (routes-auth.ts:1547-1588) is explicitly documented as 'admin-triggered, bypasses email' for emergency use, and hashes+writes the new password directly to authAccount. It does NOT call auth.api.revokeUserSessions (unlike grant-super-admin at line 1356 and create-user-temp-password at line 730, which both explicitly revoke sessions for exactly this reason) and does not set mustChangePassword: true.
findings.impact: If the reason for an 'emergency' reset is a compromised account (the primary use case for this endpoint), an attacker who already holds a valid session cookie/token for that account keeps full access after the reset — the emergency reset does not actually evict them. This defeats the endpoint's stated purpose.
findings.recommendation: After the password update, call auth.api.revokeUserSessions({ body: { userId } }) (non-fatal try/catch, matching the pattern used elsewhere in this file) and set mustChangePassword: true so the user must re-authenticate with the new credential on next use.

findings.title: E2E auth bypass ships a hardcoded default secret
findings.detail: getE2eAuthBypassSecret() (line 35-37) falls back to the literal DEFAULT_E2E_AUTH_BYPASS_SECRET ('local-e2e-auth-bypass-secret') when E2E_AUTH_BYPASS_SECRET is unset, and isServerE2eAuthBypassEnabled() only gates on NODE_ENV !== 'production' (not VERCEL_ENV). Next.js production builds (next build && next start, what Vercel runs for every deployed environment including preview/dev/uat aliases) always set NODE_ENV=production, so today this fallback is reachable only under next dev (true local dev), not on any Vercel-hosted environment.
findings.impact: Currently low risk given Vercel's NODE_ENV=production behavior for all deployed environments, but this is a latent landmine: if the build/start invocation ever changes (custom start script, containerized deploy, non-Vercel host) such that NODE_ENV isn't 'production' while E2E_AUTH_BYPASS=true and E2E_AUTH_BYPASS_SECRET is unset, anyone who knows the checked-in default string can set the hilo-e2e-auth-bypass cookie to that value and mint a super_admin session (getE2eAuthBypassUser defaults to role: 'super_admin' when no user cookie is present).
findings.recommendation: Require E2E_AUTH_BYPASS_SECRET to be explicitly set (throw/warn loudly if E2E_AUTH_BYPASS=true but the secret env var is absent) rather than silently falling back to a checked-in constant; also gate on VERCEL_ENV !== 'production' / 'preview' as defense-in-depth.

findings.title: bootstrap-admin has a TOCTOU race that could mint two super_admins
findings.detail: POST /bootstrap-admin (line 298-348) is unauthenticated by design (no super_admin exists yet) and checks existingAdmins.length > 0 before creating a new super_admin, but the check-then-act is not transactional. Two concurrent requests can both pass the SELECT before either INSERT/UPDATE commits.
findings.impact: In the narrow window before the very first super_admin is provisioned, two different unauthenticated callers hitting this endpoint concurrently could each successfully bootstrap a super_admin account rather than the second being rejected with 403. Low real-world exploitability (one-time setup step) but the 'at most one bootstrap wins' invariant is not actually enforced.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the check + auth.api.createUser call in a DB transaction with a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a bootstrap sentinel row, or use an atomic UPDATE ... WHERE NOT EXISTS pattern.

result.notes: Enumerated every file under the owned slice: src/server/middleware/auth.ts, src/lib/auth.ts, src/lib/auth-access.ts, src/lib/auth-permissions.ts, src/lib/auth-client.ts, src/lib/auth-url.ts, src/lib/rbac/platform-capabilities.ts (+test), src/lib/e2e-auth-bypass.ts, src/app/api/auth/[...all]/route.ts+helpers.ts, src/app/api/auth/ok/route.ts, src/server/routes/routes-auth.ts (full 2415 lines), and the full src/server/oauth/ directory plus src/app/oauth/consent/page.tsx. The Zapier OAuth 2.0/PKCE subsystem (authorize/token/me/action-gate/scope-registry/trigger-registry) is unusually well-hardened — constant-time comparisons, argon2id+pepper for client secrets, single-use auth codes burned before mint, refresh-token rotation with bounded reuse-grace and replay revocation, strict tenant scoping, compile-time registry/scope parity — no defects found there. src/lib/rbac/platform-capabilities.ts is explicitly self-documented as 'not yet wired to enforcement' (deliberate future-migration placeholder), so its deny-by-default design not being enforced anywhere is by design, not a bug. Verified the session-cookie token-splitting logic in middleware/auth.ts (readSessionTokenCookieValue splitting on '.') against Better Auth's actual cookie format (token.signature, confirmed via node_modules/better-auth/dist/cookies/index.mjs in a sibling project) — correct, not a defect. The two top findings both concern routes-auth.ts endpoints that bypass the tenant-scoping / session-revocation patterns the same file establishes correctly elsewhere for sibling endpoints, making the omission clearly a gap rather than an intentional design choice.

findings.title: Cross-tenant PII/financial data leak: 30+ GET endpoints resolve flightSchoolId from the URL locationId without verifying it belongs to the caller's own org
findings.detail: The helper resolveFlightSchoolFromLocation() (line 2963) is documented as 'tenant-guard-exempt: pure resolver — every caller compares the result to the session orgId before using it.' That invariant is violated by ~34 read routes and 2 write routes that call it but never compare the resolved flightSchoolId against the caller's session orgId (via resolveOrgIdFromSession). Confirmed call sites lacking the check include: GET /locations/:locationId/students/:studentId/payment-cards (line 23400, returns Stripe payment card data), .../payment-history (24457), .../documents (25856), .../logbook (11092), .../audit (10337), .../holds (10601), .../certificates (43119), .../notes (36751), .../endorsements (36393), .../invoices (16942), .../lenders (24415), .../flags (42900); GET /locations/:locationId/enrollments (6555) and /classes/:classId/enrollments (6614) — student names/emails; GET /locations/:locationId/payroll (37475) — instructor pay data, only requireAuth (any role); GET /locations/:locationId/admins (40336) — admin names/emails, only requireAuth; GET /locations/:locationId/customers (39793) and /crm-contacts (43264); GET .../instructors/document-compliance* (25736, 25765, 25812) and /students/document-compliance* (8617, 8693, 25594); POST /locations/:locationId/students/:studentId/force-document-upload (26666, requireAdmin) — writes to another org's student record; POST /locations/:locationId/notifications (42723) — writes a notification into another org's location. All of these only validate isUuid(locationId) (format) and that flightSchoolId is non-null (location exists) — never that it equals the requester's own organization. Contrast with correctly-guarded sibling routes in the same file, e.g. POST /locations/:locationId/customers (39834) and PUT/DELETE /locations/:id (2792, 2839), which use findByIdUnscoped + loc.flightSchoolId !== orgId checks.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user of ANY tenant (school) — including a low-privilege student or instructor account — can read another tenant's student payment cards, payment history, document uploads, logbooks, audit trails, holds, certificates, private notes, endorsements, invoices, lender info, compliance flags, instructor payroll figures, and the school's admin roster, by supplying an arbitrary valid locationId/studentId UUID pair for a different organization. Two write paths let a cross-tenant admin force a document-upload flag onto another school's student, and any authenticated user can inject spam/phishing notifications into another school's location. This is a direct multi-tenant data-isolation breach (aviation training/PII/financial data) and would violate FAA-adjacent compliance and PDD-005 (auth middleware centralization) intent.
findings.recommendation: Add the standard org-ownership check to every listed call site: resolve authUser/orgId via resolveOrgIdFromSession, then compare flightSchoolId !== orgId and return 404 on mismatch, immediately after resolving flightSchoolId. Given the number of affected sites, replace resolveFlightSchoolFromLocation with a single helper resolveAndVerifyFlightSchool(locationId, authUser, c) that performs both steps atomically, then update all 61 call sites so no caller can forget the check again. Also correct the misleading 'tenant-guard-exempt' comment at line 2963 once callers are fixed — it currently asserts a false invariant that let this drift in unnoticed.

findings.title: DELETE /locations/:id and PUT /locations/:id only require requireAuth() — any org role (student, instructor) can deactivate or rename the school's location
findings.detail: Lines 2792 (PUT) and 2839 (DELETE) declare requireAuth() with no {roles: [...]} restriction. requireAuth() (src/server/middleware/auth.ts:153) accepts any authenticated role when options.roles is omitted. The DELETE handler does soft-delete (sets status to 'inactive' per the comment at line 2838) and does correctly check flightSchoolId !== orgId for tenant scoping, but performs no role check — so a low-privileged member of the correct org (e.g. a student account) can deactivate the entire flight school location or edit its name/address/contact info.
findings.impact: A compromised or malicious low-privilege account (student/instructor) within a legitimate org can take the school's location offline (soft-delete) or corrupt its contact/address data, a business-critical operation that should be admin-gated.
findings.recommendation: Change both routes to requireAuth({ roles: ['admin', 'super_admin'] }) or requireAdmin(), consistent with the 14 other routes in this file that already use requireAdmin() for comparable destructive/administrative operations.

findings.title: 262 of 274 route handlers in this file use requireAuth() with no role restriction, including many mutating (POST/PUT/DELETE) operations on business-sensitive resources
findings.detail: Only 14 of 274 route declarations use requireAdmin(); the rest use bare requireAuth() (262 occurrences), which per src/server/middleware/auth.ts:153-179 grants access to any authenticated role (student, instructor, admin, super_admin) when no roles option is passed. Combined with the tenant-isolation gaps above, many business-configuration, payroll, and student-record mutation endpoints are reachable by low-privilege roles as long as they belong to (or, per the finding above, don't even need to belong to) the right org.
findings.impact: Widens the blast radius of the tenant-isolation bug above and independently allows low-privilege same-org users to perform actions likely intended for admins only (e.g. payroll viewing, location edit/delete already flagged). Without a full per-route role audit this is reported as a pattern to review rather than an exhaustive list.
findings.recommendation: Audit each requireAuth()-gated mutating route in this file against its intended actor (student vs instructor vs admin) and tighten to requireAuth({roles:[...]}) or requireAdmin() where the operation is administrative. Prioritize payroll, location settings, and admin-roster endpoints first since those were confirmed above.

findings.title: Weekly-outreach confirm endpoint inserts schedule events with zero conflict/capacity checking
findings.detail: POST /weekly-outreach/:runId/instructors/:instructorId/confirm (routes-ai-schedule.ts:3574-3683) reads `record.proposedScheduleJson.events` and inserts each into schedule_events in a plain for-loop (line 3621-3634) with NO double-booking check against existing events, NO instructor max-daily-hours check, NO operational-hours check, and no db.transaction wrapping the loop (unlike /publish and /publish-selected, which both use db.transaction and go through the constraint solver's isEntityFree/entityHoursOnDate guards). Any student/instructor/aircraft conflict already present, or introduced by two outreach runs confirmed concurrently, is inserted unchecked.
findings.impact: An instructor confirming their proposed weekly schedule can silently double-book themselves, a student, or an aircraft against events already on the live calendar (added since the proposal was generated) or against another outreach run confirmed around the same time. Because there's no transaction, a mid-loop failure also leaves a partial set of events committed with no rollback.
findings.recommendation: Route the proposed events through the same runScheduleSolver validation/insert path (or at minimum reuse isEntityFree-style occupancy checks against current schedule_events) before inserting, and wrap the insert loop in db.transaction like /publish and /publish-selected do.

findings.title: Audit-log POST endpoint lets any admin caller forge performedByUserId/performedByName
findings.detail: POST /locations/:locationId/ai-schedule/audit-log (routes-ai-schedule.ts:3458-3504) takes `performedByUserId` and `performedByName` directly from the request body (lines 3474-3475) instead of deriving them from `authUser` (which is already available via `c.get('authUser')`). Every other audit-log write in this file (schedule_published, schedule_generated) hardcodes 'system'/'AI Scheduler', so this endpoint is the one place a client fully controls attribution.
findings.impact: Any admin (or anything with an admin token) can write an audit-log entry claiming a different user performed an action, undermining the audit trail's evidentiary value.
findings.recommendation: Derive performedByUserId/performedByName from `authUser` server-side; if the client needs to attribute to a different subject (e.g. an instructor acting on a student's behalf), use `subjectStudentId`/`subjectStudentName` for that, not the performer fields.

findings.title: Constraint-solver occupancy helpers compare only entityId, not entityType
findings.detail: isEntityFree, entityHoursOnDate, entityEventCount, and studentLessonsOnDate (lines 2185-2250) all filter occupancy slots by `slot.entityId !== entityId` alone; entityType is stored on the slot but never checked. If a student, instructor, and aircraft/equipment row ever shared the same UUID, these helpers would report false conflicts/occupancy across entity types.
findings.impact: Purely theoretical under normal UUID generation (collision probability negligible), but the invariant is unenforced in code — a future refactor introducing non-UUID or human-chosen IDs would silently break scheduling correctness with no compiler or runtime signal.
findings.recommendation: Add `slot.entityType === expectedType` to each comparison for defense-in-depth; cheap fix, removes a latent correctness assumption.

findings.title: Client-side publish gates (conflicts, review checklist, override reason) have no server-side re-verification
findings.detail: handlePublishIntent (ai-schedule-sandbox.tsx:2948-2996) blocks publish client-side when `conflicts.length > 0`, the review checklist isn't complete, or a required override reason is empty. None of these are re-checked by POST /drafts/:draftId/publish or /publish-selected server-side — those endpoints only check `requireAdmin()` and blindly insert whatever events are in the draft's `scheduleEvents` payload, including any `_conflict` events.
findings.impact: Any direct API call (bypassing the UI — a compromised admin session, a scripted call, or a future UI bug) can publish conflicting/unreviewed events straight to the live schedule with no server-side guard.
findings.recommendation: At minimum, have /publish and /publish-selected re-run an overlap check against `schedule_events` for the events being inserted (similar to the existing-events occupancy logic already implemented in runScheduleSolver) and reject/flag conflicting ones rather than trusting client-computed conflict state.

findings.title: Draft weekStart/date-range fallbacks use UTC calendar day, not the location's timezone
findings.detail: POST /drafts (weekStart default, line 425), POST /drafts/instructor-create (weekStart default, line 1152), and existing-events/generate date-range iteration (lines 355-360, 2280-2286) all derive 'today' or date-range boundaries via `new Date().toISOString().split('T')[0]` or `new Date(`${d}T00:00:00`)` — UTC-anchored — while the rest of the AI-schedule domain (utcToLocalHour/localHourToUtcDate, the sandbox UI's dateToStr) is explicitly location-timezone-aware. For a location like America/Phoenix (UTC-7), a request between midnight UTC and 7am UTC (5pm-midnight local the prior day) computes 'today' one calendar day ahead of the location's actual local date.
findings.impact: Draft names/labels or default week-start values can be off by one day for schools west of UTC during evening hours; low impact since these are mostly fallback/display fields (draft events themselves carry an explicit `date` from the client), but it's the same class of bug the codebase has fixed elsewhere via the utcToLocalHour helpers.
findings.recommendation: Route these fallbacks through the location's timezone (already loaded via locationRepository.findByIdMinimal in the same request in most cases) instead of raw UTC `Date`/`toISOString()`.

findings.title: Publish and publish-selected event-insert loops are not batched — N sequential awaited inserts inside one transaction
findings.detail: Both /drafts/:draftId/publish (lines 812-834) and /publish-selected (lines 1290-1312) insert schedule_events one row at a time in a for-loop with `await tx.insert(...).returning()` per event, rather than a single batched `.values([...])` insert.
findings.impact: For a large weekly draft (potentially dozens to 100+ events), this serializes N round-trips to Postgres inside one transaction, increasing transaction hold time and publish latency proportionally to event count.
findings.recommendation: Switch to a single batched insert (`tx.insert(schema.scheduleEvents).values(toPublish.map(...)).returning()`) — Drizzle supports multi-row insert natively; this also shrinks the transaction's lock window.

result.notes: Enumerated every file in the owned slice: routes-ai-schedule.ts (3810 lines, all routes + shared solver read in full), ai-schedule-sandbox.tsx (8743 lines — all ~4200 lines of hooks/handlers/logic read in full; remaining ~4500 lines are JSX render, spot-checked for embedded handler bugs, none found), ai-schedule-sandbox-navigation.ts (43 lines, clean), and both lib/ai-sandbox files (canvas-colors.ts, port-labels.ts — trivial constant/formatter modules, clean). No CRITICAL findings. The two most actionable items are the weekly-outreach confirm endpoint's missing conflict/transaction safety and the audit-log attribution spoofing — both are concrete, fixable gaps in an otherwise carefully-guarded route file (most routes correctly use verifyLocationAccess + requireAdmin/requireAuth, and the constraint solver's occupancy logic is thorough).

findings.title: Hour logging silently misattributes to course index 0 when no active course exists
findings.detail: In `applyHoursToActiveTrainingPlanCourse` (lines 233-241) and `advanceTrainingPlanAfterCheckride` / `manuallyActivateNextTrainingPlanCourse` (lines 357-365, 469-477), the active-course index is computed as `Number.isInteger(currentCourseIndex) ? clamp(...) : Math.max(0, courseAllocations.findIndex(a => a.status === 'active'))`. When no allocation has status 'active' (e.g. plan freshly created and never manually activated, or every course finished and none advanced), `findIndex` returns -1, and `Math.max(0, -1)` silently resolves to index 0 — the first course in the array — regardless of its real status (could be completed, upcoming, or hours_complete).
findings.impact: Flight/ground/simulator hours logged for a student can be silently credited to the wrong certificate allocation (e.g. a completed Private Pilot course instead of the actual in-progress Instrument rating). This corrupts flightHoursUsed/groundHoursUsed/simulatorHoursUsed on the wrong course, which feeds training-hour guardrails, payment schedules, and quote/invoice totals — a hard-to-detect data integrity bug with financial and FAA hour-tracking consequences. Confirmed live call sites: src/server/routes/routes-locations.ts (~lines 11446, 19985, 20081, 20290) and src/server/routes/routes-checkrides.ts:317.
findings.recommendation: When findIndex returns -1 (no active course and no valid stored index), return an explicit failure (applied: false, or a distinct reason like 'no_active_course') instead of defaulting to index 0. Callers should surface this as an operator-visible error rather than silently applying hours to an arbitrary course.

findings.title: Local-timezone 'today' compared against UTC-anchored date strings in schedule status logic
findings.detail: getCourseScheduleStatus (training-plan-course-schedule.ts, line 108) and getStatus (training-plan-payment-schedule-view.ts, line 108) both compute 'today' via date.getFullYear()/getMonth()/getDate() — local server timezone getters — then string-compare against startDate/endDate/dueDate values that are date-only strings elsewhere parsed as UTC midnight (parseDateOnly in the same course-schedule file explicitly uses T00:00:00.000Z). If the server's local timezone is behind UTC (e.g. US timezones), local 'today' can differ from the UTC calendar date by hours around midnight.
findings.impact: A course or payment installment can flip between upcoming/scheduled/due/overdue/past_target up to several hours early or late relative to the intended UTC-anchored day boundary. This is a duplicated bug pattern reproduced independently in two files rather than one isolated slip.
findings.recommendation: Compute 'today' the same way parseDateOnly treats stored dates — via UTC getters or toISOString().slice(0,10) — and factor the logic into one shared helper both files import.

findings.title: Fee-definition rows summing above their parent fee item silently over-allocate to certificates without correction
findings.detail: In buildTrainingPlanCertificateCosts (lines 128-147), when a fee item has definitions (per-certificate splits), the code sums definitionTotalCents and only corrects for itemAmountCents > definitionTotalCents (excess routed to unallocatedFeeCents). There is no symmetric handling for definitionTotalCents > itemAmountCents — if per-certificate definition amounts sum to more than the parent fee item's total, each certificate still receives its full definition amount with no scaling or flag.
findings.impact: allocatedFeeCents (and each certificate's feeAmount/totalAmount) can overstate the true fee total relative to itemAmountCents, and plannedTotal will not reconcile against the actual fee item amounts. This surfaces as an inflated per-certificate quote total with no integrity check catching it.
findings.recommendation: When definitionTotalCents > itemAmountCents, either proportionally scale each definition's contribution down to match itemAmountCents, or treat it as a data-integrity error and route the excess to unallocatedFeeCents / log a warning rather than silently over-allocating.

findings.title: Instruction vs. equipment hour mismatch silently masked by Math.max instead of surfaced as a discrepancy
findings.detail: getCertificateHours (lines 141-150) computes both instructionHours and equipmentHours per bucket, expected to be equal per the documented pricing model in training-plan-allocation-adjustments.ts ('Instruction and equipment lines intentionally receive the same hour total'). Instead of asserting/reconciling equality, it takes Math.max(instructionHours, equipmentHours), silently discarding whichever side is smaller.
findings.impact: If a bug elsewhere ever causes instruction and equipment hours to diverge for a certificate, this function hides the discrepancy in the generated quote rather than surfacing it, making the underlying bug harder to detect from the customer-facing document.
findings.recommendation: When instructionHours !== equipmentHours beyond a small epsilon, log/flag the discrepancy in addition to picking a display value, so the underlying data bug is discoverable instead of silently smoothed over in the PDF.

findings.title: Index-position pairing between previous/next hour-item arrays is an unenforced invariant
findings.detail: buildTrainingPlanAllocationIncreaseLineItems (lines 405-412) pairs nextItems[index] with previousItems[index] purely by array position, not by any stable id/key. Its only current caller (routes-locations.ts:12938) passes pricingImpact.hourItems (produced by calculateTrainingPlanAllocationPurchase, which preserves array order/length via .map()) as nextItems and the original storedHourItems as previousItems, so pairing is correct today — but this is an implicit contract enforced by caller discipline, not by the function's types or logic.
findings.impact: If a future caller passes a nextItems array that has been reordered, filtered, or had items inserted/removed between snapshots (plausible given the codebase's pattern of appending new purchase lines elsewhere, e.g. calculateTrainingPlanCatalogProductPurchase), this function would silently mispair unrelated line items — either missing genuinely added hours or fabricating phantom 'additional hours' on an invoice line.
findings.recommendation: Pair items by a stable identifier instead of raw array index, or add a runtime assertion that previousItems.length === nextItems.length and that paired items share the same groupSourceId/bucket before computing addedHours.

result.note: Verified at src/server/routes/routes-micamp.ts L397-435. The findFirst at L404-406 filters only by eq(studentPaymentMethods.id, cardId) — no studentId/authUser ownership check and no flightSchoolId admin check. Proceeds to call MiCamp deleteToken (L414-417) and delete the DB row (L425-427) unconditionally once any card with that id is found. Any authenticated user (requireAuth() only) who knows/enumerates a card UUID can delete another student's stored payment method cross-tenant. Severity CRITICAL is appropriate (IDOR + IDOR-triggered external side effect via deleteToken, IDOR + cross-tenant financial-instrument destruction).

Verified against src/server/routes/routes-micamp.ts and src/server/middleware/auth.ts directly. All cited line ranges match: POST /micamp/cards (L281-288), GET /micamp/cards (L358-359), POST /micamp/payments (L441-448), GET /micamp/payments (L561-562), POST /micamp/connect (L88-95), PUT /micamp/config (L248), POST /micamp/disconnect (L219) all take flightSchoolId/studentId straight from client-supplied body/query with zero ownership check. requireAuth()/requireAdmin() (auth.ts L153-306) confirmed to check only session validity + role membership — never binds authUser.id or the caller's own school to the resource IDs in the request. authUser is used only to stamp audit fields (connectedByUserId L147, processedByUserId L538), confirmed via Read. The GET /micamp/cards 'ownership check' at L368-374 is literally 'does a row exist matching these client-supplied params', not 'does this card belong to the caller' — matches the finding's characterization exactly. Confirmed the remediation pattern (resolveOrgIdFromSession/managedSchoolId) exists elsewhere in the codebase (helpers.ts, flag-guard.ts, auth.ts) and is genuinely absent from routes-micamp.ts (zero references). This is a billing-locked, real-money surface per CLAUDE.md protected-paths — CRITICAL severity is correct as filed.

findings.title: curriculumBuilder Inngest job never transitions to 'failed' on error — stuck 'building' forever
findings.detail: The `generate-curriculum` step (curriculumBuilder.ts:109-185) has no try/catch, and the function has `retries: 0` with no `onFailure` handler registered in functions/index.ts. If the Claude call throws (rate limit, API error), or `safeParseAIJson` throws, or the parsed JSON lacks `stages` (line 153-157 throws 'AI returned an invalid curriculum structure'), the DB row's `status` stays at 'building' (set at line 100) — it is never updated to 'failed'.
